Multi-agent cooperation through in-context co-player inference

Marissa A. Weis Affiliation: Google, Paradigms of Intelligence Team    Maciej Wołczyk Affiliation: Google, Paradigms of Intelligence Team    Rajai Nasser Affiliation: Google, Paradigms of Intelligence Team    Rif A. Saurous Affiliation: Google, Paradigms of Intelligence Team    Blaise Agüera y Arcas Affiliation: Google, Paradigms of Intelligence Team Affiliation: Santa Fe Institute    João Sacramento Affiliation: Google, Paradigms of Intelligence Team    Alexander Meulemans Affiliation: Google, Paradigms of Intelligence Team Affiliation: Equal contribution
Abstract

Achieving cooperation among self-interested agents remains a fundamental challenge in multi-agent reinforcement learning. Recent work showed that mutual cooperation can be induced between “learning-aware” agents that account for and shape the learning dynamics of their co-players. However, existing approaches typically rely on hardcoded, often inconsistent, assumptions about co-player learning rules or enforce a strict separation between “naive learners” updating on fast timescales and “meta-learners” observing these updates. Here, we demonstrate that the in-context learning capabilities of sequence models allow for co-player learning awareness without requiring hardcoded assumptions or explicit timescale separation. We show that training sequence model agents against a diverse distribution of co-players naturally induces in-context best-response strategies, effectively functioning as learning algorithms on the fast intra-episode timescale. We find that the cooperative mechanism identified in prior work—where vulnerability to extortion drives mutual shaping—emerges naturally in this setting: in-context adaptation renders agents vulnerable to extortion, and the resulting mutual pressure to shape the opponent’s in-context learning dynamics resolves into the learning of cooperative behavior. Our results suggest that standard decentralized reinforcement learning on sequence models combined with co-player diversity provides a scalable path to learning cooperative behaviors.

1 Introduction

The development of foundation model agents is rapidly shifting the landscape of artificial intelligence from isolated systems to interacting autonomous agents (Xi et al., 2023; Park et al., 2023; Aguera Y Arcas et al., 2026). As these sequence-model-based agents are deployed in increasingly complex environments, they inevitably face multi-agent interactions where outcomes depend on interactions of multiple entities. Because these interactions frequently involve competing goals, ensuring that self-interested agents robustly cooperate in mixed-motive settings remains an important open challenge, even as individual agent capabilities have grown significantly.

Decentralized Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) addresses the problem of learning to interact with other agents while only having access to local observations. However, decentralized MARL is challenging due to two primary factors: equilibrium selection and non-stationarity of the environment (Shoham & Leyton-Brown, 2008; Hernandez-Leal et al., 2017). In general-sum games, many Nash equilibria may exist, and agents independently optimizing their own rewards frequently converge to suboptimal outcomes, such as mutual defection in social dilemmas (Claus & Boutilier, 1998; Foerster et al., 2018). Furthermore, from the perspective of a single agent, the environment is non-stationary because other agents are simultaneously learning and adapting their policies (Hernandez-Leal et al., 2017). Since standard single-agent reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms assume stationarity, they often fail to learn effective policies in these decentralized settings (Foerster et al., 2018; Claus & Boutilier, 1998).

To address this non-stationarity, co-player learning awareness enables agents to anticipate the learning dynamics of other agents and shape their co-players’ learning toward more beneficial equilibria (Foerster et al., 2018; Lu et al., 2022; Duque et al., 2024; Aghajohari et al., 2024b; Cooijmans et al., 2023; Balaguer et al., 2022; Khan et al., 2024; Willi et al., 2022; Xie et al., 2021; Meulemans et al., 2025a; Aghajohari et al., 2024a; Segura et al., 2025; Piche et al., 2025). These approaches generally fall into two categories. The first explicitly models the co-player’s learning update, estimating a shaping gradient by differentiating through the opponent’s update step (Foerster et al., 2018; Duque et al., 2024; Aghajohari et al., 2024b; Cooijmans et al., 2023; Willi et al., 2022; Aghajohari et al., 2024a; Piche et al., 2025). However, this requires rigid assumptions about the opponent’s learning rule and creates inconsistencies if the opponent is also learning-aware. The second category implicitly learns to shape opponents by extending the RL time horizon to encompass multiple update steps of the co-player (Lu et al., 2022; Khan et al., 2024; Meulemans et al., 2025a; Segura et al., 2025). While effective, this requires a separation of agents into “naive learners” (who update parameters frequently) and “meta-learners” (who update slowly), effectively treating the interaction as a meta-learning problem (Bengio et al., 1990; Schmidhuber, 1987; Hochreiter et al., 2001).

Meulemans et al. (2025a) describe a three-step mechanism explaining why co-player learning awareness leads to the learning of cooperative behaviors among self-interested agents:

  1. 1.

    Extortion of naive learners: The optimal strategy against a naive learner (an agent updating its policy to maximize rewards on a fast timescale) is extortion (Press & Dyson, 2012). A learning-aware meta-agent shapes the interaction so the naive learner updates its policy towards more cooperation, allowing the meta-agent to exploit the resulting behavior.

  2. 2.

    Mutual extortion leads to cooperation: When two agents with such extortionate capabilities face each other, their attempts to shape the learning of one another result in both agents learning more cooperative strategies.

  3. 3.

    Heterogeneity is key: Consequently, cooperation emerges when agents are trained in a mixed population of naive learners and learning-aware agents. Interactions with naive learners provide the gradient pressure to learn extortion (avoiding mutual defection), while interactions with learning-aware agents refine this into mutual cooperation.

We argue that the complex mechanisms employed by current co-player learning-aware methods, such as explicit naive learners and meta learners, or differentiating through co-players’ learning updates, are unnecessary for learning cooperative behaviors. We hypothesize that training sequence model agents via decentralized MARL against a diverse distribution of co-players naturally yields in-context best-response policies. These policies exhibit goal-directed adaptation through in-context learning within a single episode. Crucially, we show that this acts as a functional drop-in replacement for the “naive learner” parameter updates of prior work. Because in-context learning occurs on a fast timescale within the episode, agents become susceptible to extortion by other learning agents using in-weight updates. Consequently, the cooperative gradient dynamics identified by Meulemans et al. (2025a) emerge: gradients incentivizing the extortion of in-context learners pull agents away from pure defection, while mutual extortion gradients drive them toward cooperation.

Our contributions are as follows. We introduce a decentralized MARL setup where sequence model agents are trained against a mixed pool of diverse co-players and demonstrate that this training distribution induces strong in-context co-player inference capabilities and thereby the mutual extortion pressures leading to cooperation. We show that this setup leads to robust cooperation in the Iterated Prisoner’s Dilemma without the distinction between meta and inner trajectories, or assumptions about opponent learning rules. By bridging in-context learning and co-player learning-awareness, we provide a scalable path toward cooperative multi-agent systems using standard sequence modeling and RL. We introduce a new RL method that leverages self-supervised learning of predictive sequence models, which is well-suited to learn the in-context best-response policies required for the mixed pool training. We provide a theoretical characterization of the training equilibrium of this method, and relate it to Nash equilibria and subjective embedded equilibria (Meulemans et al., 2025b).

2 Problem setup and methods

Partially observable stochastic games. We formalize the multi-agent interaction as a partially observable stochastic game (Kuhn, 1953, POSG;) of NN agents. Each agent ii receives at each timestep an observation oti∈𝒪io^{i}_{t}\in\mathcal{O}^{i} and reward rti∈ℛir^{i}_{t}\in\mathcal{R}^{i}, and executes an action ati∈𝒜ia^{i}_{t}\in\mathcal{A}^{i}, with 𝒪i\mathcal{O}^{i}, ℛi\mathcal{R}^{i} and 𝒜i\mathcal{A}^{i} being finite sets. Policies are conditioned on the interaction history x≤ti={(oki,ak−1i,rk−1i)}k=1tx^{i}_{\leq t}=\{(o^{i}_{k},a^{i}_{k-1},r_{k-1}^{i})\}_{k=1}^{t}. We denote the policy of agent ii as πi​(ati∣x≤ti;ϕi)\pi^{i}(a^{i}_{t}\mid x^{i}_{\leq t};\phi^{i}), parameterized by ϕi\phi^{i}.

The iterated prisoner’s dilemma. We focus on the Iterated Prisoner’s Dilemma (IPD), a canonical model for studying cooperation among self-interested agents (Rapoport, 1974; Axelrod & Hamilton, 1981). In each round tt, two agents choose simultaneously to cooperate (C) or defect (D), i.e., ati∈{C,D}a_{t}^{i}\in\{\mathrm{C},\mathrm{D}\}, receiving payoffs as detailed in Tab. 1. This structure creates a social dilemma: in a single-shot game, mutual defection is the unique Nash equilibrium, even though mutual cooperation yields higher global and individual returns. While the infinitely iterated game allows for cooperative Nash equilibria, converging to these equilibria via decentralized reinforcement learning remains challenging (Foerster et al., 2018; Claus & Boutilier, 1998). For computational tractability, we approximate the infinite horizon with a fixed horizon of T=100T=100 steps, which is sufficient for the small-scale policy networks used in this work to approximate infinite-horizon behavior.

Mixed pool training. To induce robust in-context inference capabilities, we train agents within a mixed population rather than against a single fixed opponent. The training pool consists of (i) Learning Agents which use a sequence model policy that processes the full episode history x≤tix^{i}_{\leq t} and whose parameters are learned during training, and (ii) static Tabular Agents parameterized by a 5-dimensional vector, defining the probability of cooperating in the initial state and in response to the four possible joint action outcomes of the previous turn (at−1i,at−1−i)(a_{t-1}^{i},a_{t-1}^{-i}). During training, a learning agent plays 50%50\% of its episodes against another learning agent and 50%50\% against a tabular agent sampled uniformly from the parameter space. Crucially, agents do not receive agent identifiers; they must infer the nature and strategy of their opponent solely from the interaction history x≤tix^{i}_{\leq t}.

We investigate two learning algorithms for the learning agents in our pool:

Independent A2C. We employ Advantage Actor-Critic (A2C) (Mnih et al., 2016) as a standard decentralized model-free RL method. Each agent independently optimizes its policy parameters ϕi\phi^{i} to maximize its own expected return, treating the other agents as part of the environment.

Predictive Policy Improvement (PPI). We introduce a model-based algorithm that leverages a sequence model predicting the joint sequence of actions, observations, and rewards, serving simultaneously as a world model and a policy prior. This method is a variation of Maximum A-Posteriori Policy Optimization (Abdolmaleki et al., 2018, MPO), inspired by the MUPI framework for multi-agent learning (Meulemans et al., 2025b), and enables efficient learning of in-context inference mechanisms through self-supervised training. Each iteration consists of (i) gathering data with the improved policy and (ii) retraining the sequence model on the newly gathered data, similar to classical policy iteration. We define the improved policy πi​(ai|x≤ti)\pi^{i}(a^{i}|x^{i}_{\leq t}) as follows:

πi​(ai|x≤ti)∝pϕii​(ai|x≤ti)⋅exp⁡(β​Q^pi​(x≤ti,ai)),\pi^{i}(a^{i}|x^{i}_{\leq t})\propto p^{i}_{\phi^{i}}(a^{i}|x^{i}_{\leq t})\cdot\exp\left(\beta\hat{Q}_{p^{i}}(x^{i}_{\leq t},a^{i})\right), (1)

where β\beta is an inverse temperature hyperparameter. The action value Q^p​(h,a)\hat{Q}_{p}(h,a) is estimated via Monte Carlo rollouts performed within the sequence model pϕp_{\phi}. We deploy this improved policy πi​(ai|x≤ti)\pi^{i}(a^{i}|x^{i}_{\leq t}) in the games interacting with other agents, collecting a new batch of trajectories. We end the iteration by retraining the sequence model pϕiip^{i}_{\phi^{i}} on all accumulated trajectory batches of the current and previous iterations, distilling the improved behavior of πi\pi^{i} into the parameters ϕi\phi^{i}. We initialize the sequence model pϕp_{\phi} by pretraining on interactions between randomly sampled tabular agents. Refer to App. A for the implementation details, App. C for a theoretical derivation and motivation of PPI, and App. D for a theoretical analysis of the equilibrium behavior of PPI agents.

3 Results

Our central hypothesis is that training the learning agents against a diverse distribution of co-players necessitates the development of two distinct capabilities: (i) inferring the co-player’s policy from interaction history, and (ii) adapting to a best response within a single episode. We posit that this in-context best-response policy makes the agent vulnerable to extortion, reproducing the “naive learner” dynamics described by Meulemans et al. (2025a). This leads to learning pressures towards extortion policies, and subsequently, the mutual extortion between learning agents drives the agents toward cooperative policies. Interestingly, in this setup, the learning agents simultaneously occupy two roles traditionally separated in the literature: they are “naive learners” on the fast timescale (via in-context learning) and “learning-aware agents” on the slow timescale (via weight updates).

In this section, we first demonstrate that mixed-pool training indeed leads to robust cooperation without explicit time-scale separations or meta-gradient machinery. We then dissect the underlying mechanism, showing that (1) mixed pool training induces in-context best-response policies, (2) these policies are vulnerable to extortion, and (3) mutual extortion pressures resolve into learning cooperative behaviors.

3.1 Mixed training induces robust cooperation

As shown in Figure 1, both PPI and A2C agents trained in the mixed pool setup converge to cooperation in IPD. To verify this stems from the dynamics of in-context opponent inference, we perform two ablations: (1) Explicit Identification: We condition the policy on the opponent’s policy parameters (for tabular opponents) or identity flag (for other learning agents) at the start of the episode, removing the need for in-context opponent inference. (2) No mixed pool training: We train agents solely against a single other learning agent (without the tabular agent pool or structured pretraining). Without diverse opponents, agents have no incentive to develop general-purpose in-context learning mechanisms. In both ablations, agents collapse to mutual defection (c.f. Fig. 1; dashed and dotted curves). This confirms that in-context learning mechanisms—induced by the necessity to identify diverse opponents—are a critical factor enabling cooperative outcomes. Refer to App. A.4 for the ablation details.

3.2 Mechanism analysis: From in-context learning to cooperation

We now deconstruct the learning of cooperative behavior into three distinct steps, validating the causal chain from diversity to in-context learning, to extortability, and finally to cooperation.

Step 1: Diversity induces in-context best-response mechanisms. First, we verify that training against the tabular pool cultivates in-context learning. We evaluate a PPI agent trained solely against the tabular agents pool. Figure 2B plots the agent’s performance against specific tabular policies over the course of an episode. The agent rapidly adapts to the best response for the specific opponent. This confirms the emergence of in-context best-response mechanisms that perform goal-directed adaptation on the fast timescale of the episode.

Step 2: In-context learners are vulnerable to extortion. Next, we establish that such in-context best-response policies are susceptible to shaping by other co-players. We freeze the agent from Step 1, termed the "Fixed In-Context Learner" (Fixed-ICL), and train a new PPI agent solely against it. The new agent learns to extort the Fixed-ICL policy (Fig. 2C&D) (Press & Dyson, 2012). By exploiting the Fixed-ICL’s tendency to adapt, the new agent forces it into unfair cooperation, maximizing the new agent’s own reward at the expense of the Fixed-ICL. This confirms that goal-directed adaptation within the episode provides the necessary gradient signal for opponents to learn extortionate behaviors via weight updates.

Step 3: Mutual extortion drives cooperation. We initialize two agents with the extortion policies learned in Step 2 and train them against each other. Within an episode, both extortion policies shape each others in-context learning dynamics into more cooperative behavior (Fig. 2F). This push towards more cooperation is then picked up by the parameter updates, further driving both policies towards cooperative behavior (Fig. 2E), mirroring the "mutual shaping" effect observed in explicit learning-aware methods (Lu et al., 2022; Meulemans et al., 2025a).

Step 4: Synthesis in mixed populations. Mixed-pool training combines these dynamics by forcing agents to maintain in-context adaptation for tabular opponents, which renders them vulnerable to mutual extortion by other learners, ultimately driving the learning agents toward cooperation through mutual extortion (Sec. 3.1; Fig. 1 & Fig. 3). Figure 4 in Appendix B.2 shows similar results for A2C learning agents.

4 Conclusion

In this work, we have demonstrated that the complex machinery of explicit co-player learning-awareness—such as meta gradients or rigid timescale separation—is not required to learn cooperative behaviors in general-sum games. Instead, we found that simply training agents against a diverse distribution of co-players suffices to induce in-context best-response strategies. This in-context learning renders agents susceptible to shaping and consequently driving them toward cooperative behaviors through mutual extortion dynamics. Crucially, this result bridges the gap between multi-agent reinforcement learning and the training paradigms of modern foundation models. Since foundation models naturally exhibit in-context learning and are trained on diverse tasks and behaviors, our findings suggest a scalable and computationally efficient path for the emergence of cooperative social behaviors using standard decentralized learning techniques.

Appendix A Additional details on methods

A.1 Partially observable stochastic games

We formalize the multi-agent interaction as a partially observable stochastic game (Kuhn, 1953, POSG;) defined by the tuple (ℐ,𝒮,𝒜,Pt,Pr,Pi,𝒪,Po,γ,T)(\mathcal{I},\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},P_{t},P_{r},P_{i},\mathcal{O},P_{o},\gamma,T). Here, ℐ={1,…,n}\mathcal{I}=\{1,\dots,n\} is the set of nn agents. At each time step tt, the environment is in state st∈𝒮s_{t}\in\mathcal{S}. Agents simultaneously select actions from the joint action space 𝒜=×i∈ℐ𝒜i\mathcal{A}=\times_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\mathcal{A}^{i}, transitioning the environment according to Pt​(St+1∣St,At)P_{t}(S_{t+1}\mid S_{t},A_{t}). The initial state is sampled from Pi​(s0)P_{i}(s_{0}). Each agent ii receives a reward rtir^{i}_{t} from the joint factorized distribution Pr=×i∈ℐPri(ri∣s,a)P_{r}=\times_{i\in\mathcal{I}}P_{r}^{i}(r^{i}\mid s,a), and an observation otio^{i}_{t} from the observation space 𝒪=×i∈ℐ𝒪i\mathcal{O}=\times_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\mathcal{O}^{i} via the distribution Po​(ot∣st,at−1)P_{o}(o_{t}\mid s_{t},a_{t-1}). We denote the discount factor by γ\gamma and the horizon by TT. We use the superscript ii to denote variables specific to agent ii, and −i-i for the remaining agents. Policies are conditioned on the interaction history x≤ti={(oki,ak−1i,rk−1i)}k=1tx^{i}_{\leq t}=\{(o^{i}_{k},a^{i}_{k-1},r_{k-1}^{i})\}_{k=1}^{t}. We denote the policy of agent ii as πi​(ati∣x≤ti;ϕi)\pi^{i}(a^{i}_{t}\mid x^{i}_{\leq t};\phi^{i}), parameterized by ϕi\phi^{i}.

A.2 Environment

Iterated Prisoners Dilemma (IPD)

In each round both agents can output two possible actions: cooperate (CC) and defect (DD). As such, the environment emits five possible observations: the initial observation s0s_{0} and four observations based on the actions the two players took in the previous round: (C,C),(C,D),(D,C),(D,D)(C,C),(C,D),(D,C),(D,D). The state sts_{t} is then comprised of all past observations o≤to_{\leq t}. While the tabular agents are only conditioned on the latest observation oto_{t}, the PPI and A2C agents leverage the full history x≤tx_{\leq t}. Each game consists of 100 rounds. Each agent observes the state of the previous round from a first person view, i.e., its own action is enumerated first. In every round, each agent receives a reward following the payoff matrix in Tab. 1.

A.3 Agent implementations

A.3.1 PPI agents

Predictive Policy Improvement (PPI) agents, our practical approximation of embedded Bayesian agents (Meulemans et al., 2025b), combine a learned sequence model with a planning-based policy improvement mechanism.

Sequence Model Architecture.

The sequence model is a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) with a 128-dimensional hidden state. Inputs—comprising observations, actions, and rewards—are processed via modality-specific linear layers to project them into a shared 32-dimensional embedding space; observations and actions are one-hot encoded prior to projection. These embeddings serve as inputs to the GRU, and we apply the Swish activation function (Ramachandran et al., 2017) on the output. Distinct linear output heads decode the hidden states to predict future tokens for each modality.

Training Objectives.

We train the sequence model iteratively for 30 phases. In each phase, the model parameters ϕ\phi are re-initialized and trained on a dataset of interaction histories 𝒟={x(n)}n=1N\mathcal{D}=\{x^{(n)}\}^{N}_{n=1} to minimize the next-token prediction loss:

Ltrain\displaystyle L_{\text{train}} =λobs​Lobs+λact​Laction+λrew​Lreward,\displaystyle=\lambda_{\text{obs}}L_{\text{obs}}+\lambda_{\text{act}}L_{\text{action}}+\lambda_{\text{rew}}L_{\text{reward}}\,, (2)
Lobs\displaystyle L_{\text{obs}} =−1N​T∑n=1N∑t=1Tlogpϕ(ot(n)|x≤t−1(n)),\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{NT}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log p_{\phi}(o^{(n)}_{t}|x_{\leq t-1}^{(n)})\,, (3)
Lreward\displaystyle L_{\text{reward}} =−1N​T∑n=1N∑t=1Tlogpϕ(rt(n)|x≤t−1(n),ot(n)),\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{NT}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log p_{\phi}(r^{(n)}_{t}|x_{\leq t-1}^{(n)},o^{(n)}_{t})\,, (4)
Laction\displaystyle L_{\text{action}} =−1N​T∑n=1N∑t=1Tlogpϕ(at(n)|x≤t−1(n),ot(n),rt(n)).\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{NT}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log p_{\phi}(a^{(n)}_{t}|x_{\leq t-1}^{(n)},o^{(n)}_{t},r^{(n)}_{t})\,. (5)

𝒟\mathcal{D} comprises of the interaction histories from all previous and current phases. This is a common strategy in performative prediction (Perdomo et al., 2020) to ensure more stable training of the prediction model.

We model pϕ​(at∣x≤t)p_{\phi}(a_{t}\mid x_{\leq t}) and pϕ​(ot∣x<t,at−1)p_{\phi}(o_{t}\mid x_{<t},a_{t-1}) using a categorical distribution, yielding a standard categorical cross-entropy loss and we model pϕ​(rt∣x<t,at−1,ot)p_{\phi}(r_{t}\mid x_{<t},a_{t-1},o_{t}) with a normal distribution with fixed variance, yielding the mean-square error loss (r−r^)2(r-\hat{r})^{2}. In each phase, we sample 20 00020\,000 trajectories, which are concatenated with samples from previous phases for joint training of the sequence model. Optimization is performed using AdamW (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2017) (learning rate 10−410^{-4}, weight decay 10−210^{-2}, β1=0.9\beta_{1}=0.9, β2=0.98\beta_{2}=0.98) for 10 epochs with a batch size of 256. Gradients are clipped at a norm of 1.0.

Pre-training

The sequence model is pretrained on an initial dataset 𝒟0\mathcal{D}_{0} of 200 000200\,000 sample trajectories of two random tabular agents playing IPD against each other for 100 rounds using the same training hyperparameters as outlined above.

Inference

During deployment, the agent estimates Q values by performing Monte Carlo roll-outs for 15 rounds into the future using the learned sequence model as a simulator. The final action selection follows a policy π⁡(a|x≤t)\pi(a|x_{\leq t}) that re-weights the model’s prior probability p⁡(a|x≤t;ϕ)p(a|x_{\leq t};\phi) by the estimated value Q^p​(x≤t,a)\hat{Q}^{p}(x_{\leq t},a) derived from the roll-outs:

π⁡(a|x≤t)=1Z​p​(a|x≤t;ϕ)​exp⁡(β​Q^p​(x≤t,a)).\pi(a|x_{\leq t})=\frac{1}{Z}p(a|x_{\leq t};\phi)\exp(\beta\hat{Q}^{p}(x_{\leq t},a))\,. (6)

We use β=0.01\beta=0.01 for all experiments.

A.3.2 Model-free agent

Architecture

We implement an Advantage Actor-Critic (A2C) agent (Mnih et al., 2016) using a GRU-based sequence model with the same configuration as for the PPI agents. The GRU takes as input the history of observations of previous rounds and outputs the next action. The GRU is further augmented with a linear output head to estimate the value function V⁡(x)V(x). During training, we estimate the advantage A⁡(x≤t,at)A(x_{\leq t},a_{t}) using bootstrapped temporal-difference errors:

A⁡(x≤t,at)=rt+γ​V​(x≤t+1)−V⁡(x≤t).A(x_{\leq t},a_{t})=r_{t}+\gamma V(x_{\leq t+1})-V(x_{\leq t})\,.

The model parameters are updated to minimize the combined policy gradient and value estimation loss:

L=∑t=1T(CLOSE\displaystyle L=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\bigg( −log⁡π⁡(at|x≤t)​A​(x≤t,at)\displaystyle-\log\pi(a_{t}|x_{\leq t})A(x_{\leq t},a_{t})
+cv​(rt+γ​V​(x≤t+1)−V⁡(x≤t))2\displaystyle+c_{v}\left(r_{t}+\gamma V(x_{\leq t+1})-V(x_{\leq t})\right)^{2}
+ce∑iπ(ati|x≤t)logπ(ati|x≤t)),\displaystyle+c_{e}\sum_{i}\pi(a_{t}^{i}|x_{\leq t})\log\pi(a_{t}^{i}|x_{\leq t})\bigg)\,,

where cv,cec_{v},c_{e} are hyperparameters representing, correspondingly, the value function and entropy training coefficients.

Training

To get comparable results, we follow the A2C training protocol from Meulemans et al. (2025a) including the value function estimation, Generalized Advantage Estimation (Schulman et al., 2015), advantage normalization and reward scaling. See Appendix A of Meulemans et al. (2025a) for details.

For each experiment, we perform a hyperparameter search over the learning rate, GAE lambda, advantage normalization, reward scaling and entropy regularization. We report the hyperparameters corresponding to the best-performing setting in Table 2.

A.3.3 Tabular agents

Tabular agents employ a memory-1 policy defined by five parameters: the cooperation probabilities conditional on the previous outcome (c​c,c​d,d​c,d​dcc,cd,dc,dd) and the initial state (s0s_{0}). Each parameter is initialized from a uniform distribution 𝒰⁡(0,1)\mathcal{U}(0,1).

A.4 Ablations

A.4.1 Policy conditioning

For the “Opponent ID” ablation (Fig. 1), we prepend the observation sequence 𝐱≤t\mathbf{x}_{\leq t} with a conditioning vector 𝐳\mathbf{z} representing the opponent’s identity. For tabular agents, 𝐳\mathbf{z} is defined as the flattened vector of log-probabilities across all possible observations o∈𝒪o\in\mathcal{O}:

𝐳=(log⁡π⁡(a|o))o∈𝒪,a∈𝒜\mathbf{z}=\big(\log\pi(a|o)\big)_{o\in\mathcal{O},a\in\mathcal{A}}

where 𝒪={(C,C),(C,D),(D,C),(D,D),Start}\mathcal{O}=\{(C,C),(C,D),(D,C),(D,D),\text{Start}\}. For A2C and PPI agents, 𝐳=0\mathbf{z}=\textbf{0}.

A.4.2 No mixed pool training

For the “No Tabular Opponents” ablation (Fig. 1), we remove the tabular opponents from the mixed agent pool for both PPI and A2C experiments. For PPI, we additionally change the pretraining data distribution D0D_{0} to not include tabular agents but instead consist of purely random action sequences with the corresponding rewards.

Appendix B Additional results

B.1 In-episode trajectories for mixed pool training

Figure 3 shows the performance of PPI and A2C within a single episode during early training in the mixed pool setting (c.f. Sec. 3.1), i.e., for phase=8\text{phase}=8 for PPI and training iteration=70​k\text{training iteration}=70k for A2C, showing the emergence of in-context opponent inference and an initial gradient towards cooperation against other learning agents.

B.2 Additional results on A2C

Figure 4 shows A2C-based results, corresponding to the PPI results presented in Figure 2 in the main text. In Step 1, we observe that an A2C agent learns to implement best response against a variety of tabular agents, same as for PPI. In Step 2, however, we observe that the newly trained A2C agent manages to get a higher reward playing against the Fixed-ICL baseline than the PPI agent (correspondingly, ∼1.25\sim 1.25 vs. ∼0.9\sim 0.9). This can either be caused by (i) the PPI Fixed-ICL policy being harder to exploit or (ii) A2C finding a better exploiter policy. The irregular shape of the exploitation dynamics in Figure 4D suggests that the A2C exploiter agent learned a complex adversarial strategy against the A2C Fixed-ICL policy. In contrast, the PPI extortion policy of Figure 2D seems to be a more regular extortion policy. Finally, in Step 3, the A2C agents initially move towards cooperation but due to training instability they might still turn back to defection depending on the seed.

Appendix C Derivation of Predictive Policy Improvement (PPI)

In this section, we provide a formal derivation of the Predictive Policy Improvement (PPI) algorithm. PPI is inspired by the theoretically grounded MUPI framework (Meulemans et al., 2025b), and is closely related to Maximum a Posteriori Policy Optimization (Abdolmaleki et al., 2018, MPO;). PPI departs from standard MPO by replacing the separate value function and self-model of MPO with a single sequence model trained in a self-supervised fashion to predict actions, observations and rewards. This model serves simultaneously as a world model and a policy prior, leveraging the generative capabilities of sequence models for value estimation and policy representation.

C.1 Objective: The Variational Lower Bound

We consider an agent optimizing its policy π\pi to maximize the expected return V⁡(π)=𝔼τ∼ℙπ​[∑t=0Tγt​rt]V(\pi)=\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\mathbb{P}_{\pi}}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{T}\gamma^{t}r_{t}\right]. To avoid notational clutter, we omit the agent-specific superscripts, as this derivation applies equally to the single-agent setting. We introduce a parameterized sequence model pϕ​(a∣x≤t)p_{\phi}(a\mid x_{\leq t}) which acts as a behavioral prior or self-model over the interaction history x≤tx_{\leq t}. We define a surrogate objective JJ by penalizing the KL-divergence between the behavioral policy π\pi and the prior pϕp_{\phi}:

J(π,ϕ)=𝔼τ∼ℙπ[∑t=0Tγtrt−αKL(π(⋅∣x≤t)||pϕ(⋅∣x≤t))].J(\pi,\phi)=\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\mathbb{P}_{\pi}}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{T}\gamma^{t}r_{t}-\alpha\mathrm{KL}\left(\pi(\cdot\mid x_{\leq t})\,||\,p_{\phi}(\cdot\mid x_{\leq t})\right)\right]. (7)

Since KL(⋅||⋅)≥0\mathrm{KL}(\cdot||\cdot)\geq 0, J⁡(π,ϕ)J(\pi,\phi) is a strict lower bound on V⁡(π)V(\pi), with equality at π=pϕ\pi=p_{\phi}. We optimize this bound via coordinate ascent on π\pi (the non-parametric policy) and ϕ\phi (the parametric sequence model).

C.2 Step 1: Non-parametric Policy Improvement w.r.t. π\pi

Optimizing J⁡(π,ϕ)J(\pi,\phi) w.r.t. π\pi for a fixed ϕ\phi is a full-fledged optimal control problem, which generally lacks an analytical solution and is therefore ill-suited for direct non-parametric policy improvement. Instead, we use a first-order approximation of J⁡(π,ϕk)J(\pi,\phi_{k}) around π=pϕk\pi=p_{\phi_{k}}, where pϕkp_{\phi_{k}} is the self-model trained on the dataset gathered by deploying the previous policy πk−1\pi_{k-1}:

J¯​(π,ϕk)=∑t=1T𝔼x≤t∼ℙpϕk[𝔼a∼π(⋅∣x≤t)[Qpϕk(x≤t,a)]−αKL(π(⋅∣x≤t)||pϕk(⋅∣x≤t))−Vpϕk(x≤t)]+J(pϕk,ϕk).\begin{split}\bar{J}(\pi,\phi_{k})&=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{x_{\leq t}\sim\mathbb{P}_{p_{\phi_{k}}}}\Big[\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi(\cdot\mid x_{\leq t})}\left[Q^{p_{\phi_{k}}}(x_{\leq t},a)\right]-\alpha\mathrm{KL}\left(\pi(\cdot\mid x_{\leq t})\,||\,p_{\phi_{k}}(\cdot\mid x_{\leq t})\right)\\ &\quad-V^{p_{\phi_{k}}}(x_{\leq t})\Big]+J(p_{\phi_{k}},\phi_{k}).\end{split} (8)

Note that here, the Q-value is equal to the unregularized value Qpϕk(x≤t,a)=𝔼τ>t∼ℙpϕk(⋅∣x≤t,a)[∑t′=tTγt′−trt′]Q^{p_{\phi_{k}}}(x_{\leq t},a)=\mathbb{E}_{\tau_{>t}\sim\mathbb{P}_{p_{\phi_{k}}}(\cdot\mid x_{\leq t},a)}\left[\sum_{t^{\prime}=t}^{T}\gamma^{t^{\prime}-t}r_{t^{\prime}}\right], as all KL terms evaluate to zero under the prior. The crucial difference between JJ and J¯\bar{J} is that the expectation over histories in J¯\bar{J} does not depend on the policy π\pi being optimized, which permits a closed-form solution for arg⁡maxπ⁡J¯\arg\max_{\pi}\bar{J}.

We proceed to show that J¯\bar{J} is indeed a first-order approximation to JJ around pϕkp_{\phi_{k}} via the following two lemmas.

Lemma C.1.

J¯​(pϕk,ϕk)=J⁡(pϕk,ϕk)\bar{J}(p_{\phi_{k}},\phi_{k})=J(p_{\phi_{k}},\phi_{k})

Proof.

It is easy to see that the terms of equation 8 inside the expectation cancel out when π=pϕk\pi=p_{\phi_{k}}, leaving only J⁡(pϕk,ϕk)J(p_{\phi_{k}},\phi_{k}). ∎

Lemma C.2.

∇πJ¯​(π,ϕk)|π=pϕk=∇πJ​(π,ϕk)|π=pϕk\nabla_{\pi}\bar{J}(\pi,\phi_{k})|_{\pi=p_{\phi_{k}}}=\nabla_{\pi}J(\pi,\phi_{k})|_{\pi=p_{\phi_{k}}}

Proof.

We analyze the functional derivatives of both objectives with respect to the policy distribution π⁡(a∣x≤t)\pi(a\mid x_{\leq t}) evaluated at a specific history x≤tx_{\leq t} and action aa.

First, consider the surrogate objective J¯​(π,ϕk)\bar{J}(\pi,\phi_{k}). Because the expectation over histories is fixed to the prior distribution ℙpϕk\mathbb{P}_{p_{\phi_{k}}} and thus does not depend on the optimization variable π\pi, the functional derivative is straightforward. Applying the product rule to the logarithmic term, the functional derivative with respect to the local action probability π⁡(a∣x≤t)\pi(a\mid x_{\leq t}) is:

δ​J¯​(π,ϕk)δ​π​(a∣x≤t)=ℙpϕk​(x≤t)​(Qpϕk​(x≤t,a)−α​log⁡π⁡(a∣x≤t)pϕk​(a∣x≤t)−α).\frac{\delta\bar{J}(\pi,\phi_{k})}{\delta\pi(a\mid x_{\leq t})}=\mathbb{P}_{p_{\phi_{k}}}(x_{\leq t})\left(Q^{p_{\phi_{k}}}(x_{\leq t},a)-\alpha\log\frac{\pi(a\mid x_{\leq t})}{p_{\phi_{k}}(a\mid x_{\leq t})}-\alpha\right). (9)

Evaluating this derivative at the prior π=pϕk\pi=p_{\phi_{k}}, the logarithmic term vanishes (since log⁡1=0\log 1=0), yielding:

δ​J¯​(π,ϕk)δ​π​(a∣x≤t)|π=pϕk=ℙpϕk​(x≤t)​(Qpϕk​(x≤t,a)−α).\left.\frac{\delta\bar{J}(\pi,\phi_{k})}{\delta\pi(a\mid x_{\leq t})}\right|_{\pi=p_{\phi_{k}}}=\mathbb{P}_{p_{\phi_{k}}}(x_{\leq t})\left(Q^{p_{\phi_{k}}}(x_{\leq t},a)-\alpha\right). (10)

Next, differentiating the true objective J⁡(π,ϕk)J(\pi,\phi_{k}) is more involved because π\pi dictates the history visitation distribution ℙπ​(x≤t)\mathbb{P}_{\pi}(x_{\leq t}). We define the regularized Q-function, Qregπ​(x≤t,a)Q^{\pi}_{\mathrm{reg}}(x_{\leq t},a), which captures the expected return including all future KL penalties, but excluding the immediate penalty at time tt:

Qregπ(x≤t,a)=𝔼τ>t∼ℙπ(⋅∣x≤t,a)[∑k=tTγk−tRk−α∑k=t+1Tγk−tKL(π(⋅∣x≤k)||pϕk(⋅∣x≤k))].Q^{\pi}_{\mathrm{reg}}(x_{\leq t},a)=\mathbb{E}_{\tau_{>t}\sim\mathbb{P}_{\pi}(\cdot\mid x_{\leq t},a)}\left[\sum_{k=t}^{T}\gamma^{k-t}R_{k}-\alpha\sum_{k=t+1}^{T}\gamma^{k-t}\mathrm{KL}\left(\pi(\cdot\mid x_{\leq k})\,||\,p_{\phi_{k}}(\cdot\mid x_{\leq k})\right)\right]. (11)

Using this, the value of a specific history is:

Vregπ​(x≤t)=∑a′π⁡(a′∣x≤t)​(Qregπ​(x≤t,a′)−α​log⁡π⁡(a′∣x≤t)pϕk​(a′∣x≤t)).V^{\pi}_{\textrm{reg}}(x_{\leq t})=\sum_{a^{\prime}}\pi(a^{\prime}\mid x_{\leq t})\left(Q^{\pi}_{\mathrm{reg}}(x_{\leq t},a^{\prime})-\alpha\log\frac{\pi(a^{\prime}\mid x_{\leq t})}{p_{\phi_{k}}(a^{\prime}\mid x_{\leq t})}\right). (12)

To find the functional derivative of the global objective JJ with respect to the local policy π⁡(a∣x≤t)\pi(a\mid x_{\leq t}), we apply the continuous extension of the Performance Difference Lemma (Kakade & Langford, 2002). This theorem establishes that the indirect effect of the policy on the visitation distribution ℙπ​(x≤t)\mathbb{P}_{\pi}(x_{\leq t}) yields a net zero contribution to the gradient. Consequently, the derivative isolates the state visitation probability multiplied by the local derivative of the value function:

δ​J​(π,ϕk)δ​π​(a∣x≤t)=ℙπ​(x≤t)​∂Vπ​(x≤t)∂π⁡(a∣x≤t).\frac{\delta J(\pi,\phi_{k})}{\delta\pi(a\mid x_{\leq t})}=\mathbb{P}_{\pi}(x_{\leq t})\frac{\partial V^{\pi}(x_{\leq t})}{\partial\pi(a\mid x_{\leq t})}. (13)

Taking the partial derivative of Vπ​(x≤t)V^{\pi}(x_{\leq t}) yields:

δ​J​(π,ϕk)δ​π​(a∣x≤t)=ℙπ​(x≤t)​(Qregπ​(x≤t,a)−α​log⁡π⁡(a∣x≤t)pϕk​(a∣x≤t)−α).\frac{\delta J(\pi,\phi_{k})}{\delta\pi(a\mid x_{\leq t})}=\mathbb{P}_{\pi}(x_{\leq t})\left(Q^{\pi}_{\mathrm{reg}}(x_{\leq t},a)-\alpha\log\frac{\pi(a\mid x_{\leq t})}{p_{\phi_{k}}(a\mid x_{\leq t})}-\alpha\right). (14)

Finally, we evaluate this true derivative at the prior policy π=pϕk\pi=p_{\phi_{k}}. Three simplifications occur:

  • •

    The history visitation distribution matches the prior: ℙπ​(x≤t)=ℙpϕk​(x≤t)\mathbb{P}_{\pi}(x_{\leq t})=\mathbb{P}_{p_{\phi_{k}}}(x_{\leq t}).

  • •

    The immediate KL penalty evaluates to zero: log⁡1=0\log 1=0.

  • •

    Because the policy perfectly matches the prior at all future timesteps, all future KL penalties evaluate to zero. Consequently, the regularized Q-function smoothly collapses to the unregularized Q-function of the prior: Qregπ​(x≤t,a)=Qpϕk​(x≤t,a)Q^{\pi}_{\mathrm{reg}}(x_{\leq t},a)=Q^{p_{\phi_{k}}}(x_{\leq t},a).

Applying these simplifications yields:

δ​J​(π,ϕk)δ​π​(a∣x≤t)|π=pϕk=ℙpϕk​(x≤t)​(Qpϕk​(x≤t,a)−α).\left.\frac{\delta J(\pi,\phi_{k})}{\delta\pi(a\mid x_{\leq t})}\right|_{\pi=p_{\phi_{k}}}=\mathbb{P}_{p_{\phi_{k}}}(x_{\leq t})\left(Q^{p_{\phi_{k}}}(x_{\leq t},a)-\alpha\right). (15)

Since the functional derivatives of both JJ and J¯\bar{J} evaluated at π=pϕk\pi=p_{\phi_{k}} perfectly coincide, it follows that ∇πJ¯​(π,ϕk)|π=pϕk=∇πJ​(π,ϕk)|π=pϕk\nabla_{\pi}\bar{J}(\pi,\phi_{k})|_{\pi=p_{\phi_{k}}}=\nabla_{\pi}J(\pi,\phi_{k})|_{\pi=p_{\phi_{k}}}, concluding the proof. ∎

Optimizing J¯\bar{J}.

Optimizing J¯​(π,ϕk)\bar{J}(\pi,\phi_{k}) w.r.t. π\pi for fixed ϕk\phi_{k} has the well-known Boltzmann policy as solution:

π∗​(a∣x≤t)=pϕk​(a∣x≤t)Z⁡(x≤t)​exp⁡(β​Qpϕk​(x≤t,a)),\pi^{*}(a\mid x_{\leq t})=\frac{p_{\phi_{k}}(a\mid x_{\leq t})}{Z(x_{\leq t})}\exp\left(\beta Q^{p_{\phi_{k}}}(x_{\leq t},a)\right), (16)

with the inverse temperature β=1α\beta=\frac{1}{\alpha}. We treat β\beta as a fixed hyperparameter defining a trust region around pϕkp_{\phi_{k}} where J¯\bar{J} is a sufficiently accurate approximation of JJ.

C.3 Comparison with MPO and Sequence-Model Value Estimation

While PPI shares the coordinate-ascent structure of MPO, it differs in how Q-values are obtained and whether π\pi or pϕkp_{\phi_{k}} is deployed as behavioral policy to gather trajectories. In standard MPO, Q⁡(s,a)Q(s,a) is typically represented by a separate neural network (a critic) trained via temporal difference (TD) learning on the agent’s own experience, relying on the Markov property to condition on a single state ss instead of the full history.

In contrast, PPI leverages the sequence model as a world model. The value Q^p​(x≤t,a)\hat{Q}_{p}(x_{\leq t},a) is estimated via Monte Carlo rollouts performed within the sequence model itself. By sampling future trajectories τ>t\tau_{>t} from pϕ(⋅∣x≤t,a)p_{\phi}(\cdot\mid x_{\leq t},a), the agent evaluates the expected return of an action based on its internal representation of both the environment dynamics and the co-player’s predicted responses. This allows PPI to benefit from the high-capacity temporal dependencies captured by the sequence model. Note that PPI is easily extendable toward learning an explicit Q-value function conditioned on full histories to amortize the cost of the MC rollouts and reduce variance.

Appendix D Theoretical Analysis of the Equilibrium Behavior of PPI Agents

In this section, we analyze the theoretical properties of the Predictive Policy Improvement (PPI) algorithm. Unlike standard reinforcement learning, where agents optimize a policy against a fixed (or stationarily adapting) environment, PPI agents operate in a performative loop: the agent’s predictive model determines its policy, which determines the data distribution, which in turn is used to update the predictive model. This is closely related to the concept of “performative prediction” (Perdomo et al., 2020), where the predictions of a model can affect the distribution of the very data it is trying to predict (with traffic prediction models being a prominent example).

We formalize this interaction and define the concept of a Predictive Equilibrium (PE). We show that while a global pure-strategy equilibrium is not guaranteed to exist due to the non-convex nature of deep neural networks, a local predictive equilibrium (consistent with gradient-based optimization) and a mixed predictive equilibrium (randomized strategies) are guaranteed to exist under standard assumptions. Finally, we show that in the limit of a perfect world model, a predictive equilibrium corresponds to a subjective embedded equilibrium (Meulemans et al., 2025b).

D.1 Formal Setup

Consider a game with nn agents. Each agent ii maintains a predictive sequence model pθi​(hi)p_{\theta_{i}}(h^{i}) parameterized by θi∈Θi\theta_{i}\in\Theta_{i}, where hih^{i} is a history x≤tix^{i}_{\leq t} of arbitrary length tt, and Θi\Theta_{i} is a compact metric space (e.g., a bounded subset of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}).

The Performative Loop.

The PPI algorithm (Algorithm 1) induces a closed-loop dependency between parameters and data:

  1. 1.

    Model induces Policy: The agent derives a policy πθi\pi_{\theta_{i}} from its model pθip_{\theta_{i}} via the policy improvement operator, defined in Eq. 6 (the Boltzmann policy over Q-values estimated via rollout).

  2. 2.

    Policy induces Data: When all agents interact using policies 𝝅𝜽={πθ1,…,πθN}\bm{\pi}_{\bm{\theta}}=\{\pi_{\theta_{1}},\dots,\pi_{\theta_{N}}\}, they induce a joint distribution over interaction histories hh. We denote the true probability distribution of histories generated by the current joint configuration 𝜽\bm{\theta} as ℙ⁡(⋅,𝜽)\mathbb{P}(\cdot;\bm{\theta}).

  3. 3.

    Data induces Model: The agent updates θi\theta_{i} to minimize the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between the observed distribution ℙ⁡(⋅,𝜽)\mathbb{P}(\cdot;\bm{\theta}) and its model pθip_{\theta_{i}}.

D.2 Predictive Equilibria

A stable point of this training loop is a configuration where the model optimally predicts the data generated by the policy derived from that very model.

Definition D.1 (Global Predictive Equilibrium).

A joint configuration 𝜽∗=(θ1∗,…,θn∗)\bm{\theta}^{*}=(\theta^{*}_{1},\dots,\theta^{*}_{n}) is a Global Predictive Equilibrium if, for all agents ii:

θi∗∈arg​minθi∈ΘiKL(ℙ(hi;𝜽∗)||pθi(hi)).\displaystyle\theta^{*}_{i}\in\argmin_{\theta_{i}\in\Theta_{i}}\text{KL}\left(\mathbb{P}(h_{i};\bm{\theta}^{*})\,||\,p_{\theta_{i}}(h_{i})\right)\,. (17)

Intuitively, at equilibrium, no agent can improve their world model given the behavior induced by the current joint models.

Challenges.

Proving the existence of a global PE is difficult because the map θ↦πθ\theta\mapsto\pi_{\theta} is complex and the resulting objective is generally non-convex. The “argmin” set may change discontinuously (mode hopping), preventing the application of standard fixed-point theorems. To address this, we define two relaxed solution concepts: Local PE (relevant to gradient descent) and Mixed PE.

D.2.1 Local Predictive Equilibrium

In practice, PPI agents update parameters via gradient descent. They do not find global minima but rather stationary points. Crucially, the update assumes that the data distribution is fixed (which can be interpreted as a “stop-gradient” on the environment dynamics).

Definition D.2 (Local Predictive Equilibrium).

Let Θi⊂ℝdi\Theta_{i}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d_{i}} be a compact, convex parameter space for each agent i∈ℐi\in\mathcal{I}. A joint configuration 𝜽∗=(θ1∗,…,θn∗)∈∏i∈ℐΘi\bm{\theta}^{*}=(\theta^{*}_{1},\dots,\theta^{*}_{n})\in\prod_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\Theta_{i} is a Local Predictive Equilibrium if, for all agents i∈ℐi\in\mathcal{I}, the configuration satisfies the first-order stationarity condition with respect to their local loss, assuming the data generating process is fixed. Formally:

⟨∇θiKL(ℙ(hi;𝜽∗)∣∣pθi(hi))|θi=θi∗,ϕi−θi∗⟩≥0,∀ϕi∈Θi,∀i∈ℐ,\displaystyle\left\langle\nabla_{\theta_{i}}\mathrm{KL}\left(\mathbb{P}(h_{i};\bm{\theta}^{*})\mid\mid p_{\theta_{i}}(h_{i})\right)\Big|_{\theta_{i}=\theta^{*}_{i}},\phi_{i}-\theta^{*}_{i}\right\rangle\geq 0\,,\quad\forall\phi_{i}\in\Theta_{i}\,,\forall i\in\mathcal{I}\,, (18)

where ⟨⋅,⋅⟩\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle denotes the standard inner product.

This variational inequality definition corresponds precisely to the convergence criteria of projected gradient descent in the PPI algorithm. If θi∗\theta^{*}_{i} lies in the interior of Θi\Theta_{i}, Eq. 18 implies the standard condition

∇θiKL(ℙ(hi;𝜽∗)∣∣pθi(hi))|θi=θi∗=0,∀i∈ℐ.\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta_{i}}\mathrm{KL}\left(\mathbb{P}(h_{i};\bm{\theta}^{*})\mid\mid p_{\theta_{i}}(h_{i})\right)\Big|_{\theta_{i}=\theta^{*}_{i}}=0\,,\quad\forall i\in\mathcal{I}\,. (19)
Theorem D.3 (Existence of Local Predictive Equilibrium).

Assume Θi\Theta_{i} is a compact, convex subset of ℝdi\mathbb{R}^{d_{i}}. Assume the mapping from parameters 𝛉\bm{\theta} to the local gradient of the loss Gi(𝛉)=∇ϑKL(ℙ(⋅;𝛉)∣∣pϑ)|ϑ=θiG_{i}(\bm{\theta})=\nabla_{\vartheta}\mathrm{KL}\left(\mathbb{P}(\cdot;\bm{\theta})\mid\mid p_{\vartheta}\right)\big|_{\vartheta=\theta_{i}} is continuous. Then, there exists at least one Local Predictive Equilibrium.

Proof.

We analyze the existence of a Local Predictive Equilibrium by framing it as a fixed-point problem. Let ℒi(𝜽,ψ)=KL(ℙ(hi;𝜽)∣∣pψ(hi))\mathcal{L}_{i}(\bm{\theta},\psi)=\mathrm{KL}\left(\mathbb{P}(h_{i};\bm{\theta})\mid\mid p_{\psi}(h_{i})\right) denote the loss function for agent ii, where the first argument 𝜽\bm{\theta} determines the data distribution (fixed locally) and the second argument ψ\psi is the parameter being optimized. Define the local gradient field G:Θ→ℝDG:\Theta\to\mathbb{R}^{D} (where D=∑i∈ℐdiD=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}d_{i}) as the concatenation of the individual gradients:

G⁡(𝜽)=(∇ψℒ1​(𝜽,ψ)|ψ=θ1,…,∇ψℒn​(𝜽,ψ)|ψ=θn).G(\bm{\theta})=\left(\nabla_{\psi}\mathcal{L}_{1}(\bm{\theta},\psi)\big|_{\psi=\theta_{1}},\dots,\nabla_{\psi}\mathcal{L}_{n}(\bm{\theta},\psi)\big|_{\psi=\theta_{n}}\right)\,.

A Local Predictive Equilibrium is characterized by the variational inequality ⟨G⁡(𝜽∗),ϕ−𝜽∗⟩≥0\langle G(\bm{\theta}^{*}),\phi-\bm{\theta}^{*}\rangle\geq 0 for all ϕ∈Θ\phi\in\Theta, where Θ=∏i∈ℐΘi\Theta=\prod_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\Theta_{i}.

We assume the parameter space Θ\Theta is a compact, convex subset of Euclidean space, and that the gradient field G⁡(𝜽)G(\bm{\theta}) is continuous. The continuity of GG follows naturally from the smoothness assumptions on the predictive models pθp_{\theta} and the induced policy distributions.

Consider the map T:Θ→ΘT:\Theta\to\Theta defined by a projected gradient step:

T⁡(𝜽)=ProjΘ​(𝜽−η​G​(𝜽)),T(\bm{\theta})=\text{Proj}_{\Theta}\left(\bm{\theta}-\eta G(\bm{\theta})\right)\,,

where η>0\eta>0 is a scalar step size and ProjΘ\text{Proj}_{\Theta} is the Euclidean projection onto the set Θ\Theta.

  1. 1.

    Compactness and Convexity: By assumption, Θ\Theta is a compact and convex set.

  2. 2.

    Continuity: The map GG is continuous by assumption. The projection operator ProjΘ\text{Proj}_{\Theta} is non-expansive and thus continuous. Therefore, the composition TT is a continuous map from Θ\Theta to itself.

By Brouwer’s Fixed Point Theorem, there exists a point 𝜽∗∈Θ\bm{\theta}^{*}\in\Theta such that T⁡(𝜽∗)=𝜽∗T(\bm{\theta}^{*})=\bm{\theta}^{*}. This fixed point condition implies:

𝜽∗=ProjΘ​(𝜽∗−η​G​(𝜽∗)).\bm{\theta}^{*}=\text{Proj}_{\Theta}\left(\bm{\theta}^{*}-\eta G(\bm{\theta}^{*})\right)\,.

By the standard property of the Euclidean projection onto a closed convex set, this equation holds if and only if:

⟨(𝜽∗−η​G​(𝜽∗))−𝜽∗,ϕ−𝜽∗⟩≤0,∀ϕ∈Θ.\langle\left(\bm{\theta}^{*}-\eta G(\bm{\theta}^{*})\right)-\bm{\theta}^{*},\phi-\bm{\theta}^{*}\rangle\leq 0\,,\quad\forall\phi\in\Theta\,.

Simplifying the terms inside the inner product, we obtain:

⟨−η​G​(𝜽∗),ϕ−𝜽∗⟩≤0⟹⟨G⁡(𝜽∗),ϕ−𝜽∗⟩≥0,∀ϕ∈Θ.\langle-\eta G(\bm{\theta}^{*}),\phi-\bm{\theta}^{*}\rangle\leq 0\implies\langle G(\bm{\theta}^{*}),\phi-\bm{\theta}^{*}\rangle\geq 0\,,\quad\forall\phi\in\Theta\,.

This inequality is precisely the first-order stationarity condition defined in Eq. 18, generalized to the joint parameter space Θ\Theta. Therefore, the fixed point 𝜽∗\bm{\theta}^{*} constitutes a Local Predictive Equilibrium, rigorously accommodating both interior stationary points and boundary solutions. ∎

D.2.2 Mixed Predictive Equilibrium

To guarantee the existence of an equilibrium without relying on local approximations, we can allow agents to randomize over model parameters. This is analogous to mixed strategies in game theory.

Definition D.4 (Mixed Predictive Equilibrium).

Let ΔΘi\Delta_{\Theta_{i}} be the set of probability distributions over parameters Θi\Theta_{i}. A Mixed Predictive Equilibrium is a tuple of distributions 𝝁∗=(μ1∗,…,μn∗)\bm{\mu}^{*}=(\mu^{*}_{1},\dots,\mu^{*}_{n}) such that for all i∈ℐi\in\mathcal{I}:

μi∗∈arg​minμi∈ΔΘiKL(ℙ(hi;𝝁∗)∣∣pμi(hi)),\displaystyle\mu^{*}_{i}\in\argmin_{\mu_{i}\in\Delta_{\Theta_{i}}}{\mathrm{KL}\left(\mathbb{P}(h_{i};\bm{\mu}^{*})\mid\mid p_{\mu_{i}}(h_{i})\right)}\,, (20)

where pμi​(hi)=𝔼θi∼μi​[pθi​(hi)]p_{\mu_{i}}(h_{i})=\mathbb{E}_{\theta_{i}\sim\mu_{i}}\left[p_{\theta_{i}}(h_{i})\right], and ℙ⁡(hi,𝝁∗)\mathbb{P}(h_{i};\bm{\mu}^{*}) is the distribution of histories generated when each agent ii follows the policy πμi\pi_{\mu_{i}} obtained by applying the policy improvement operator equation 6 on pμip_{\mu_{i}}.

Theorem D.5 (Existence of Mixed Predictive Equilibrium).

Assume Θi\Theta_{i} is a compact metric space11 1 It is worth noting that we do not require the convexity of Θi\Theta_{i} in Theorem D.5, we only need compactness. and the map (𝛉,θi′)↦KL(ℙ(⋅;𝛉)∣∣pθi′)(\bm{\theta},\theta_{i}^{\prime})\mapsto\mathrm{KL}\left(\mathbb{P}(\cdot;\bm{\theta})\mid\mid p_{\theta_{i}^{\prime}}\right) is continuous for every i∈ℐi\in\mathcal{I}. Furthermore, assume that KL(ℙ(hi;𝛍)∣∣pμi(hi))<∞\mathrm{KL}\left(\mathbb{P}(h_{i};\bm{\mu})\mid\mid p_{\mu_{i}}(h_{i})\right)<\infty for all 𝛍∈Δ=∏i∈ℐΔΘi\bm{\mu}\in\Delta=\prod_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\Delta_{\Theta_{i}}. Then a Mixed Predictive Equilibrium exists.

Proof.

We prove existence by constructing a continuous map on the space of mixed strategies and applying a fixed-point theorem. Let ΔΘi\Delta_{\Theta_{i}} be the space of Borel probability measures on the compact metric space Θi\Theta_{i}. Endowed with the Wasserstein metric, ΔΘi\Delta_{\Theta_{i}} is a compact, convex metric space. Let Δ=∏i∈ℐΔΘi\Delta=\prod_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\Delta_{\Theta_{i}} be the joint strategy space.

Since ΔΘi\Delta_{\Theta_{i}} is a compact metric space, it is separable. We can fix a countable dense subset Di={μ~i,k}k=1∞⊂ΔΘiD_{i}=\{\tilde{\mu}_{i,k}\}_{k=1}^{\infty}\subset\Delta_{\Theta_{i}}.

We define the continuous advantage function ai:Δ×ΔΘi→ℝ≥0a_{i}:\Delta\times\Delta_{\Theta_{i}}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} as:

ai(𝝁,μi′)=max{0,KL(ℙ(hi;𝝁)∣∣pμi(hi))−KL(ℙ(hi;𝝁)∣∣pμi′(hi))}.a_{i}(\bm{\mu},\mu^{\prime}_{i})=\max\left\{0,\mathrm{KL}\left(\mathbb{P}(h_{i};\bm{\mu})\mid\mid p_{\mu_{i}}(h_{i})\right)-\mathrm{KL}\left(\mathbb{P}(h_{i};\bm{\mu})\mid\mid p_{\mu^{\prime}_{i}}(h_{i})\right)\right\}.

Since KL(ℙ(hi;𝝁)∣∣pμi(hi))<∞\mathrm{KL}\left(\mathbb{P}(h_{i};\bm{\mu})\mid\mid p_{\mu_{i}}(h_{i})\right)<\infty, the advantage function is well-defined and evaluates to a finite real number.

We now construct a transition map Ti:Δ→ΔΘiT_{i}:\Delta\to\Delta_{\Theta_{i}}. Define a finite measure Ai​(𝝁)A_{i}(\bm{\mu}) on Θi\Theta_{i} that places weights on the dense subset DiD_{i} proportional to the advantage:

Ai​(𝝁)=∑k=1∞2−k​ai​(𝝁,μ~i,k)​μ~i,k.A_{i}(\bm{\mu})=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}2^{-k}a_{i}(\bm{\mu},\tilde{\mu}_{i,k})\tilde{\mu}_{i,k}\,.

Let Ai​(𝝁)​(Θi)=∑k=1∞2−k​ai​(𝝁,μ~i,k)A_{i}(\bm{\mu})(\Theta_{i})=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}2^{-k}a_{i}(\bm{\mu},\tilde{\mu}_{i,k}) denote its total mass. We define Ti​(𝝁)T_{i}(\bm{\mu}) by mixing the current strategy μi\mu_{i} with the improvement measure Ai​(𝝁)A_{i}(\bm{\mu}):

Ti​(𝝁)=μi+Ai​(𝝁)1+Ai​(𝝁)​(Θi).T_{i}(\bm{\mu})=\frac{\mu_{i}+A_{i}(\bm{\mu})}{1+A_{i}(\bm{\mu})(\Theta_{i})}.

Since the mappings 𝜽↦KL(ℙ(⋅;𝜽)∣∣pμi′)\bm{\theta}\mapsto\mathrm{KL}\left(\mathbb{P}(\cdot;\bm{\theta})\mid\mid p_{\mu^{\prime}_{i}}\right) are continuous and the spaces are compact, aia_{i} is uniformly bounded and continuous in 𝝁\bm{\mu} with respect to the weak-* topology. Consequently, the joint map T⁡(𝝁)=(T1​(𝝁),…,Tn​(𝝁))T(\bm{\mu})=(T_{1}(\bm{\mu}),\dots,T_{n}(\bm{\mu})) is a continuous function from the compact convex set Δ\Delta to itself. By Schauder’s fixed-point theorem, there exists a fixed point 𝝁∗∈Δ\bm{\mu}^{*}\in\Delta such that T⁡(𝝁∗)=𝝁∗T(\bm{\mu}^{*})=\bm{\mu}^{*}.

We now prove by contradiction that 𝝁∗\bm{\mu}^{*} is a Mixed Predictive Equilibrium. Let

Ci=Ai​(𝝁∗)​(Θi).C_{i}=A_{i}(\bm{\mu}^{*})(\Theta_{i})\,.

From the fixed point condition μi∗=Ti​(𝝁∗)\mu^{*}_{i}=T_{i}(\bm{\mu}^{*}), we obtain:

μi∗​(1+Ci)=μi∗+Ai​(𝝁∗)⟹Ci​μi∗=Ai​(𝝁∗).\mu^{*}_{i}\left(1+C_{i}\right)=\mu^{*}_{i}+A_{i}(\bm{\mu}^{*})\implies C_{i}\mu^{*}_{i}=A_{i}(\bm{\mu}^{*}).

Assume 𝝁∗\bm{\mu}^{*} is not a Mixed Predictive Equilibrium. Then, for some agent i∈ℐi\in\mathcal{I}, there exists a distribution μ^i∈ΔΘi\hat{\mu}_{i}\in\Delta_{\Theta_{i}} such that

KL(ℙ(hi;𝝁∗)∣∣pμ^i(hi))<KL(ℙ(hi;𝝁∗)∣∣pμi∗(hi)).\mathrm{KL}\left(\mathbb{P}(h_{i};\bm{\mu}^{*})\mid\mid p_{\hat{\mu}_{i}}(h_{i})\right)<\mathrm{KL}\left(\mathbb{P}(h_{i};\bm{\mu}^{*})\mid\mid p_{\mu^{*}_{i}}(h_{i})\right)\,.

Let

ϵ:=KL(ℙ(hi;𝝁∗)∣∣pμi∗(hi))−KL(ℙ(hi;𝝁∗)∣∣pμ^i(hi))>0.\epsilon:=\mathrm{KL}\left(\mathbb{P}(h_{i};\bm{\mu}^{*})\mid\mid p_{\mu^{*}_{i}}(h_{i})\right)-\mathrm{KL}\left(\mathbb{P}(h_{i};\bm{\mu}^{*})\mid\mid p_{\hat{\mu}_{i}}(h_{i})\right)>0\,.

By definition, the advantage of μ^i\hat{\mu}_{i} is strictly positive: ai​(𝝁∗,μ^i)=ϵ>0a_{i}(\bm{\mu}^{*},\hat{\mu}_{i})=\epsilon>0.

Now since the mapping (𝜽,θi′)↦KL(ℙ(⋅;𝜽)∣∣pθi′)(\bm{\theta},\theta_{i}^{\prime})\mapsto\mathrm{KL}\left(\mathbb{P}(\cdot;\bm{\theta})\mid\mid p_{\theta_{i}^{\prime}}\right) is continuous, it follows that the functional μi′↦KL(ℙ(hi;𝝁∗)∣∣pμi′(hi))\mu^{\prime}_{i}\mapsto\mathrm{KL}\left(\mathbb{P}(h_{i};\bm{\mu}^{*})\mid\mid p_{\mu^{\prime}_{i}}(h_{i})\right) is continuous on the compact metric space ΔΘi\Delta_{\Theta_{i}}, and hence the advantage function ai​(𝝁∗,⋅)a_{i}(\bm{\mu}^{*},\cdot) is uniformly continuous. Therefore, there exists an open neighborhood U⊂ΔΘiU\subset\Delta_{\Theta_{i}} containing μ^i\hat{\mu}_{i} such that ai​(𝝁∗,μi′)>ϵ/2a_{i}(\bm{\mu}^{*},\mu^{\prime}_{i})>\epsilon/2 for all μi′∈U\mu^{\prime}_{i}\in U.

Since the set Di={μ~i,k}k=1∞D_{i}=\{\tilde{\mu}_{i,k}\}_{k=1}^{\infty} is dense in ΔΘi\Delta_{\Theta_{i}}, there exists an integer KK such that μ~i,K∈U\tilde{\mu}_{i,K}\in U. Consequently, ai​(𝝁∗,μ~i,K)>ϵ/2>0a_{i}(\bm{\mu}^{*},\tilde{\mu}_{i,K})>\epsilon/2>0. This strictly positive advantage guarantees that the total mass of the improvement measure is strictly positive:

Ci=Ai​(𝝁∗)​(Θi)≥2−K​ai​(𝝁∗,μ~i,K)>0.C_{i}=A_{i}(\bm{\mu}^{*})(\Theta_{i})\geq 2^{-K}a_{i}(\bm{\mu}^{*},\tilde{\mu}_{i,K})>0.

From the fixed-point condition Ci​μi∗=Ai​(𝝁∗)C_{i}\mu^{*}_{i}=A_{i}(\bm{\mu}^{*}), and knowing Ci>0C_{i}>0, we can express μi∗\mu^{*}_{i} as an infinite convex combination of the basis measures in DiD_{i}:

μi∗=1Ci​Ai​(𝝁∗)=∑k=1∞wk​μ~i,k,\mu^{*}_{i}=\frac{1}{C_{i}}A_{i}(\bm{\mu}^{*})=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}w_{k}\tilde{\mu}_{i,k}\,,

where the weights wk=2−k​ai​(𝝁∗,μ~i,k)Ci≥0w_{k}=\frac{2^{-k}a_{i}(\bm{\mu}^{*},\tilde{\mu}_{i,k})}{C_{i}}\geq 0 sum to exactly 11.

Now, consider the expected predictive model under the mixed strategy μi∗\mu^{*}_{i}. By linearity of the expectation, we have:

pμi∗​(hi)=𝔼θi∼μi∗​[pθi​(hi)]=∑k=1∞wk​𝔼θi∼μ~i,k​[pθi​(hi)]=∑k=1∞wk​pμ~i,k​(hi).p_{\mu^{*}_{i}}(h_{i})=\mathbb{E}_{\theta_{i}\sim\mu^{*}_{i}}\left[p_{\theta_{i}}(h_{i})\right]=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}w_{k}\mathbb{E}_{\theta_{i}\sim\tilde{\mu}_{i,k}}\left[p_{\theta_{i}}(h_{i})\right]=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}w_{k}p_{\tilde{\mu}_{i,k}}(h_{i})\,.

Because the Kullback-Leibler divergence is strictly convex with respect to its second argument, we can apply Jensen’s inequality to the infinite convex combination:

KL(ℙ(hi;𝝁∗)∣∣pμi∗(hi))\displaystyle\mathrm{KL}\left(\mathbb{P}(h_{i};\bm{\mu}^{*})\mid\mid p_{\mu^{*}_{i}}(h_{i})\right) =KL(ℙ(hi;𝝁∗)∣∣∑k=1∞wkpμ~i,k(hi))\displaystyle=\mathrm{KL}\left(\mathbb{P}(h_{i};\bm{\mu}^{*})\mid\mid\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}w_{k}p_{\tilde{\mu}_{i,k}}(h_{i})\right)
≤∑k=1∞wkKL(ℙ(hi;𝝁∗)∣∣pμ~i,k(hi)).\displaystyle\leq\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}w_{k}\mathrm{KL}\left(\mathbb{P}(h_{i};\bm{\mu}^{*})\mid\mid p_{\tilde{\mu}_{i,k}}(h_{i})\right)\,.

Crucially, by the definition of the advantage function and the construction of the weights wkw_{k}, any weight wkw_{k} is strictly positive if and only if the corresponding advantage ai​(𝝁∗,μ~i,k)>0a_{i}(\bm{\mu}^{*},\tilde{\mu}_{i,k})>0. A strictly positive advantage exactly means that the evaluated measure achieves a strictly lower loss than the current state μi∗\mu_{i}^{*}:

KL(ℙ(hi;𝝁∗)∣∣pμ~i,k(hi))<KL(ℙ(hi;𝝁∗)∣∣pμi∗(hi)).\mathrm{KL}\left(\mathbb{P}(h_{i};\bm{\mu}^{*})\mid\mid p_{\tilde{\mu}_{i,k}}(h_{i})\right)<\mathrm{KL}\left(\mathbb{P}(h_{i};\bm{\mu}^{*})\mid\mid p_{\mu^{*}_{i}}(h_{i})\right)\,.

Since there is at least one weight wK>0w_{K}>0 with an advantage bounded away from zero by ϵ/2\epsilon/2, substituting this strict upper bound into the sum over kk yields:

∑k=1∞wkKL(ℙ(hi;𝝁∗)∣∣pμ~i,k(hi))\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}w_{k}\mathrm{KL}\left(\mathbb{P}(h_{i};\bm{\mu}^{*})\mid\mid p_{\tilde{\mu}_{i,k}}(h_{i})\right) <∑k=1∞wkKL(ℙ(hi;𝝁∗)∣∣pμi∗(hi))\displaystyle<\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}w_{k}\mathrm{KL}\left(\mathbb{P}(h_{i};\bm{\mu}^{*})\mid\mid p_{\mu^{*}_{i}}(h_{i})\right)
=KL(ℙ(hi;𝝁∗)∣∣pμi∗(hi))∑k=1∞wk\displaystyle=\mathrm{KL}\left(\mathbb{P}(h_{i};\bm{\mu}^{*})\mid\mid p_{\mu^{*}_{i}}(h_{i})\right)\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}w_{k}
=KL(ℙ(hi;𝝁∗)∣∣pμi∗(hi)).\displaystyle=\mathrm{KL}\left(\mathbb{P}(h_{i};\bm{\mu}^{*})\mid\mid p_{\mu^{*}_{i}}(h_{i})\right)\,.

Combining the inequalities together, we arrive at the following absolute contradiction:

KL(ℙ(hi;𝝁∗)∣∣pμi∗(hi))<KL(ℙ(hi;𝝁∗)∣∣pμi∗(hi)).\mathrm{KL}\left(\mathbb{P}(h_{i};\bm{\mu}^{*})\mid\mid p_{\mu^{*}_{i}}(h_{i})\right)<\mathrm{KL}\left(\mathbb{P}(h_{i};\bm{\mu}^{*})\mid\mid p_{\mu^{*}_{i}}(h_{i})\right)\,.

Therefore, our initial assumption must be false. No such superior distribution μ^i\hat{\mu}_{i} can exist, and the fixed point 𝝁∗\bm{\mu}^{*} is indeed a Mixed Predictive Equilibrium. ∎

An interesting corollary of the above theorem, is that if our model is convex in functional space, then there exists a pure global predictive equilibrium.

Corollary D.6 (Existence of Pure Predictive Equilibrium under Model Functional Convexity).

Consider the same assumptions as in Theorem D.5. Assume furthermore that for every agent i∈ℐi\in\mathcal{I}, the space of representable predictive models {pθi∣θi∈Θi}\{p_{\theta_{i}}\mid\theta_{i}\in\Theta_{i}\} is convex. That is, for every θi′,θi′′∈Θi\theta_{i}^{\prime},\theta_{i}^{\prime\prime}\in\Theta_{i} and every αi∈[0,1]\alpha_{i}\in[0,1], there exists a pure parameter θi∈Θi\theta_{i}\in\Theta_{i} satisfying pθi=αi​pθi′+(1−αi)​pθi′′p_{\theta_{i}}=\alpha_{i}p_{\theta^{\prime}_{i}}+(1-\alpha_{i})p_{\theta^{\prime\prime}_{i}}.22 2 We emphasize that we do not require convexity in the parameters, i.e., we do not require that pαi​θi′+(1−αi)​θi′′=αi​pθi′+(1−αi)​pθi′′p_{\alpha_{i}\theta_{i}^{\prime}+(1-\alpha_{i})\theta_{i}^{\prime\prime}}=\alpha_{i}p_{\theta_{i}^{\prime}}+(1-\alpha_{i})p_{\theta_{i}^{\prime\prime}}. Under these conditions, a Global Predictive Equilibrium (in pure strategies) always exists.

Proof.

From Theorem D.5, there exists a Mixed Predictive Equilibrium 𝝁∗=(μ1∗,…,μn∗)∈∏i∈ℐΔΘi\bm{\mu}^{*}=(\mu^{*}_{1},\dots,\mu^{*}_{n})\in\prod_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\Delta_{\Theta_{i}}. To establish the existence of a pure Global Predictive Equilibrium, we will demonstrate that for any probability distribution μi∈ΔΘi\mu_{i}\in\Delta_{\Theta_{i}}, the model functional convexity assumption guarantees the existence of a pure parameter θi∗∈Θi\theta_{i}^{*}\in\Theta_{i} such that pθi∗=pμi=𝔼θi∼μi​[pθi]p_{\theta_{i}^{*}}=p_{\mu_{i}}=\mathbb{E}_{\theta_{i}\sim\mu_{i}}\left[p_{\theta_{i}}\right].

We first prove this claim for finitely supported measures. Let μi=∑k=1mwk​δθi,k\mu_{i}=\sum_{k=1}^{m}w_{k}\delta_{\theta_{i,k}} be a finitely supported probability measure on Θi\Theta_{i}, where wk≥0w_{k}\geq 0 and ∑k=1mwk=1\sum_{k=1}^{m}w_{k}=1. We proceed by induction on the support size mm. The base case m=1m=1 is trivial, as pμi=pθi,1p_{\mu_{i}}=p_{\theta_{i,1}}. Assuming the claim holds for m−1m-1, we can express μi\mu_{i} (provided wm<1w_{m}<1) as:

pμi=wm​pθi,m+(1−wm)​∑k=1m−1wk1−wm​pθi,k.p_{\mu_{i}}=w_{m}p_{\theta_{i,m}}+(1-w_{m})\sum_{k=1}^{m-1}\frac{w_{k}}{1-w_{m}}p_{\theta_{i,k}}\,.

By the inductive hypothesis, there exists a pure parameter θ~i∈Θi\tilde{\theta}_{i}\in\Theta_{i} such that pθ~i=∑k=1m−1wk1−wm​pθi,kp_{\tilde{\theta}_{i}}=\sum_{k=1}^{m-1}\frac{w_{k}}{1-w_{m}}p_{\theta_{i,k}}. Applying the convexity assumption with αi=wm\alpha_{i}=w_{m}, θi′=θi,m\theta^{\prime}_{i}=\theta_{i,m}, and θi′′=θ~i\theta^{\prime\prime}_{i}=\tilde{\theta}_{i}, there exists θi∈Θi\theta_{i}\in\Theta_{i} such that pθi=wm​pθi,m+(1−wm)​pθ~i=pμip_{\theta_{i}}=w_{m}p_{\theta_{i,m}}+(1-w_{m})p_{\tilde{\theta}_{i}}=p_{\mu_{i}}. Thus, the claim holds for all finitely supported measures.

Now, consider an arbitrary measure μi∈ΔΘi\mu_{i}\in\Delta_{\Theta_{i}}. Since the set of finitely supported measures is dense in ΔΘi\Delta_{\Theta_{i}} under the weak-* topology, there exists a sequence of finitely supported measures (μi(m))m=1∞(\mu_{i}^{(m)})_{m=1}^{\infty} converging weakly to μi\mu_{i}.

Because the mapping θi↦pθi​(hi)\theta_{i}\mapsto p_{\theta_{i}}(h_{i}) is continuous and bounded for any given hih_{i}, the functional ν↦pν​(hi)=∫pθi​(hi)​𝑑ν​(θi)\nu\mapsto p_{\nu}(h_{i})=\int p_{\theta_{i}}(h_{i})d\nu(\theta_{i}) is continuous with respect to the weak-* topology. Consequently, the sequence of expected models converges pointwise: pμi(m)→pμip_{\mu_{i}^{(m)}}\to p_{\mu_{i}} as m→∞m\to\infty.

From the inductive step, for each finitely supported measure μi(m)\mu_{i}^{(m)}, there exists a corresponding pure parameter θi(m)∈Θi\theta_{i}^{(m)}\in\Theta_{i} such that pθi(m)=pμi(m)p_{\theta_{i}^{(m)}}=p_{\mu_{i}^{(m)}}. This constructs a sequence of pure parameters (θi(m))m=1∞(\theta_{i}^{(m)})_{m=1}^{\infty} in Θi\Theta_{i}. Since Θi\Theta_{i} is a compact metric space, this sequence admits a convergent subsequence (θi(mk))k=1∞(\theta_{i}^{(m_{k})})_{k=1}^{\infty} that converges to some limit point θi∗∈Θi\theta_{i}^{*}\in\Theta_{i}.

By the continuity of the map θi↦pθi\theta_{i}\mapsto p_{\theta_{i}}, we find:

pθi∗=limk→∞pθi(mk)=limk→∞pμi(mk)=pμi.p_{\theta_{i}^{*}}=\lim_{k\to\infty}p_{\theta_{i}^{(m_{k})}}=\lim_{k\to\infty}p_{\mu_{i}^{(m_{k})}}=p_{\mu_{i}}\,.

Thus, for the Mixed Predictive Equilibrium 𝝁∗\bm{\mu}^{*}, there exists a joint configuration of pure parameters 𝜽∗=(θ1∗,…,θn∗)∈∏i∈ℐΘi\bm{\theta}^{*}=(\theta^{*}_{1},\dots,\theta^{*}_{n})\in\prod_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\Theta_{i} such that pθi∗=pμi∗p_{\theta^{*}_{i}}=p_{\mu^{*}_{i}} for all i∈ℐi\in\mathcal{I}.

It then follows that

θi∗∈arg​minθi∈ΘiKL(ℙ(hi;𝜽∗)∣∣pθi(hi))∀i∈ℐ.\displaystyle\theta^{*}_{i}\in\argmin_{\theta_{i}\in\Theta_{i}}\mathrm{KL}\left(\mathbb{P}(h_{i};\bm{\theta}^{*})\mid\mid p_{\theta_{i}}(h_{i})\right)\quad\forall i\in\mathcal{I}\,.

This precisely satisfies the definition of a Global Predictive Equilibrium, proving its existence in pure strategies under these conditions. ∎

We remark that while the assumption of functional convexity is an idealization for finite-capacity networks, deep neural networks are universal function approximators; consequently, as model capacity increases, the space of representable distributions approximates the full convex set of valid probability measures, rendering the existence of a pure equilibrium an increasingly accurate approximation.

D.3 Relationship to Nash Equilibria and Subjective Embedded Equilibria

Finally, we connect the fixed points of the PPI algorithm to the standard solution concepts of game theory. In standard game theory, a Nash Equilibrium assumes that agents act optimally given a fixed environment, where the policies of co-players are independent of the focal agent’s current action selection. In contrast, agents in the PPI framework act optimally with respect to an internal world model pθip_{\theta_{i}} that estimates the joint distribution of future trajectories, thereby capturing potential reactive dependencies between the focal agent’s actions and the co-players’ responses.

This is closely related to the concept of “Embedded Equilibria”, which characterizes the equilibrium behavior that emerges from such self-predictive dynamics:

Definition D.7 (Subjective Embedded Equilibrium).

(Meulemans et al., 2025b) A joint policy profile 𝝅∗\bm{\pi}^{*} and a set of internal sequence models {p1∗,…,pn∗}\{p^{*}_{1},\dots,p^{*}_{n}\} constitute a Subjective Embedded Equilibrium if:

  1. 1.

    Subjective Optimality: Each agent’s policy πi∗\pi^{*}_{i} is a strict best-response to its internal world model pi∗p^{*}_{i}.

  2. 2.

    On-Path Consistency: Each agent’s world model perfectly matches the true environment dynamics exclusively on the equilibrium path (the distribution of histories ℙ∗\mathbb{P}^{*} genuinely generated by the joint policy 𝝅∗\bm{\pi}^{*}).

Crucially, a Subjective Embedded Equilibrium places no constraints on the accuracy of the agents’ models regarding off-path counterfactuals (actions that are assigned zero probability under 𝝅∗\bm{\pi}^{*}). Nevertheless, πi∗\pi_{i}^{*} must be a best response with respect to pi∗p_{i}^{*}, and this takes into account counterfactual off-policy paths. In other words, according to the predictive model pi∗p_{i}^{*}, the agent ii will not get higher expected returns by deviating from πi∗\pi_{i}^{*}.

We refer the reader to Meulemans et al. (2025b) for further details about subjective embedded equilibria and their properties.

It turns out that if PPI agents converge to a fixed point for which their (predictive) world models are perfect, then the predictive equilibrium corresponds to a subjective embedded equilibrium. Let us first formalize the predictive equilibrium with perfect world models:

Definition D.8 (Perfect Predictive Equilibrium).

A Perfect Predictive Equilibrium is a configuration 𝜽∗\bm{\theta}^{*} where the agents perfectly model the induced data distribution:

KL(ℙ(hi;𝜽∗)∣∣pθi∗(hi))=0∀i∈ℐ.\displaystyle\mathrm{KL}\left(\mathbb{P}(h_{i};\bm{\theta}^{*})\mid\mid p_{\theta^{*}_{i}}(h_{i})\right)=0\quad\forall i\in\mathcal{I}\,. (21)
Theorem D.9 (Perfect Predictive Equilibrium ⟹\implies Subjective Embedded Equilibrium).

Consider predictive agents using the policy improvement operator defined in Eq. 6, where πθi​(ai|hi)∝pθi​(ai|hi)​exp⁡(β​Qpθi​(hi,ai))\pi_{\theta_{i}}(a_{i}|h_{i})\propto p_{\theta_{i}}(a_{i}|h_{i})\exp(\beta Q^{p_{\theta_{i}}}(h_{i},a_{i})). If 𝛉∗\bm{\theta}^{*} is a Perfect Predictive Equilibrium, then the resulting configuration is consistent with a Subjective Embedded Equilibrium.

Proof.

At a Perfect Predictive Equilibrium, the condition KL(ℙ(⋅;𝜽∗)∣∣pθi∗(⋅))=0\mathrm{KL}\left(\mathbb{P}(\cdot;\bm{\theta}^{*})\mid\mid p_{\theta^{*}_{i}}(\cdot)\right)=0 implies that the sequence model matches the true data distribution almost everywhere. Thus, on the equilibrium path, the prior action probability generated by the sequence model exactly matches the true behavioral policy: pθi∗​(ai|hi)=πθi∗​(ai|hi)p_{\theta^{*}_{i}}(a_{i}|h_{i})=\pi_{\theta^{*}_{i}}(a_{i}|h_{i}). This immediately satisfies the On-Path Consistency condition.

Substituting pθi∗=πθi∗p_{\theta^{*}_{i}}=\pi_{\theta^{*}_{i}} into the policy improvement operator yields:

πθi∗​(ai|hi)\displaystyle\pi_{\theta^{*}_{i}}(a_{i}|h_{i}) =1Z⁡(hi)​πθi∗​(ai|hi)​exp⁡(β​Qpθi∗​(hi,ai)).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{Z(h_{i})}\pi_{\theta^{*}_{i}}(a_{i}|h_{i})\exp(\beta Q^{p_{\theta^{*}_{i}}}(h_{i},a_{i}))\,.

For any action aia_{i} in the support of the policy (where πθi∗​(ai|hi)>0\pi_{\theta^{*}_{i}}(a_{i}|h_{i})>0), we divide both sides by πθi∗​(ai|hi)\pi_{\theta^{*}_{i}}(a_{i}|h_{i}) to obtain:

1=1Z⁡(hi)​exp⁡(β​Qpθi∗​(hi,ai))⟹Qpθi∗​(hi,ai)=ln⁡Z⁡(hi)β.\displaystyle 1=\frac{1}{Z(h_{i})}\exp(\beta Q^{p_{\theta^{*}_{i}}}(h_{i},a_{i}))\implies Q^{p_{\theta^{*}_{i}}}(h_{i},a_{i})=\frac{\ln Z(h_{i})}{\beta}\,.

Since Z⁡(hi)Z(h_{i}) is a normalizing constant independent of aia_{i}, the expected return evaluated under the model must be identical for all actions played with positive probability.

Now consider any off-path action ai′a^{\prime}_{i} not in the support of the policy (where πθi∗​(ai′|hi)=0\pi_{\theta^{*}_{i}}(a^{\prime}_{i}|h_{i})=0). Because this action is never taken under the joint policy, the marginal probability ℙ⁡(hi,ai′,𝜽∗)=0\mathbb{P}(h_{i},a^{\prime}_{i};\bm{\theta}^{*})=0. Consequently, the KL divergence places absolutely no constraints on the model’s conditional predictions following ai′a^{\prime}_{i}.

To formally verify Subjective Optimality, we demonstrate that there exists a valid completion of the sequence model’s off-path conditional probabilities that justifies πθi∗​(ai′|hi)=0\pi_{\theta^{*}_{i}}(a^{\prime}_{i}|h_{i})=0. Let em​i​n=(o,rm​i​n)e_{min}=(o,r_{min}) be an environment percept containing the minimal possible reward rm​i​nr_{min}. We define the model’s off-path counterfactual completion as pθi∗​(em​i​n∣hi,ai′)=1p_{\theta^{*}_{i}}(e_{min}\mid h_{i},a^{\prime}_{i})=1, assuming absorbing minimal rewards thereafter.

Evaluating the expected return under this completed subjective model yields Qpθi∗​(hi,ai′)=Vm​i​nQ^{p_{\theta^{*}_{i}}}(h_{i},a^{\prime}_{i})=V_{min}, which is not larger than the on-path return ln⁡Z⁡(hi)β\frac{\ln Z(h_{i})}{\beta}. Because the policy operator is restricted by the prior pθi∗​(ai′|hi)p_{\theta^{*}_{i}}(a^{\prime}_{i}|h_{i}), which must evaluate to 00 to satisfy the fixed point, the agent assigns exactly 00 probability to the suboptimal deviation ai′a^{\prime}_{i}. Therefore, the agent is playing an exact, best-response to its subjective world model, fully satisfying the definition of a Subjective Embedded Equilibrium. ∎
